narrative: The model estimates your chance of failing at 17%, so failure is not certain—about one in six similar students failed—but the school treats this as enough risk to require remedial courses. The three strongest influences in your profile are actually protective, not damning. Ranked first is your record of no past class failures, which pulls the prediction toward passing. Second is your wish to continue into higher education; every passing student in this data wanted that, so it also supports passing. Third is your mother’s work as a teacher, a relatively uncommon but favorable signal. So the fail-risk is not coming from these top three; it comes from weaker factors that add up, especially eight absences against an average of about four, weekend alcohol use reported as high when only a small minority of passing students report that, and studying less than two hours weekly when most passers study two to five hours. To improve, protect your no-failure record, keep your higher-education goal, and use your mother’s support. Reduce absences, cut weekend drinking, and build a steady study routine. Remedial courses are a chance to address those accumulating risks before they outweigh your clear strengths.
